Lessons.Title: Design a Carnival Game (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Local original 2021 teacher lesson.html SHA256 8b6242caaa64209b52d046393ab321dd9655b619ca84b566646dc7434132fb81 and preparation.html SHA256 a4960ca9ca0c24de4a4b90d83505feb0044efa4253ae211d14bdd35df8c8f485 were reviewed on Our-CS. This lesson is expressly OPTIONAL: the publisher preparation says it adds no new mathematical content standards, but applies existing modelling and measurement skills. Separate original Student Task Statements PDF and three image files without descriptive alt-text were not inspected. Source-parity cannot be certified for those assets.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Carnival Games (10 minutes) is open discussion of pictured games such as penny toss and marble runs. Ask what pupils notice or wonder, what makes games challenging yet fair, how players win. Example source teacher suggestions: identical attempts and equipment, reasonable starting positions and clear rules; the source does not prescribe a single numeric winning score.

Activity1 Create Your Own Carnival Game (45 minutes): groups of FOUR get paper clips, pipe cleaners, rulers, masking/painter's tape and yardsticks. Teacher also gathers tape measures, toilet-paper tubes, marbles, pennies, paper cups and bouncing balls as applicable. Group creates its OWN playable game, describes its original rules and winning condition, and TESTS THE FIRST VERSION AT LEAST ONCE. Do not award completion merely for an unplayed written concept.

After the initial test, the original task requires redesign of the game to include AT LEAST TWO DISTINCT mathematical elements chosen from EXACTLY FOUR listed categories: (1) length or distance measurement IN INCHES; (2) elapsed TIME; (3) multiplication/division WITHIN100; (4) addition/subtraction WITHIN1,000. Students choose any two or more categories and integrate them into actual revised gameplay/scoring; there is no fixed correct combination, object length, time, score or winner.

Original student directive 'If you have time, play the new and improved game' makes a POST-REDESIGN play optional, unlike mandatory INITIAL play test. Teacher narrative suggests potential intergroup game swap if time permits. Duration may exceed60 minutes or span two days. Source initial design/testing is approximately20–25min, revision another10–15min. Do not invent a compulsory second play or a publisher-favored game.

Source synthesis: explain game rules, what it takes to win, what changed in redesign and how revised features alter fairness/strategy, to a classmate from ANOTHER group. Teacher and peers can propose further changes. The teacher reviews actual physical evidence, correct metric type, valid numeric scope, fairness, and communication rather than auto-scoring one answer.

Publisher Lesson16 local HTML has no stand-alone Cool-down section in the original lesson timeline; no publisher cooldown is represented as source copy. All original publisher visuals/PDF, compiled tests, CI, Stage D, academic approval and production runtime remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mathematical modeling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Students choose quantities, constraints, rules and winner criteria for a playable game.
KeyConcepts.Example: Design a fair marble roll game.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fair rules
KeyConcepts.Definition: Participants should share comparable equipment, starts, turn counts and known scoring.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain how a player can win before the first trial.
KeyConcepts.Example: Same starting line, three turns each.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two mathematical categories
KeyConcepts.Definition: The redesigned game integrates at least two of the source's four mathematics families.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count distinct math components, not the number of calculations.
KeyConcepts.Example: Inches of travel and elapsed seconds use two categories.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arithmetic scope
KeyConcepts.Definition: Source multiplies/divides within100 and adds/subtracts within1,000.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use arithmetic values within the specified bounds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Example design—not a publisher source answer
WorkedExamples.Question: How could a marble game use two mathematical requirements?
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose inch distances and elapsed time.
Steps: Agree on fair same start and same materials.
Play original game at least once.
Revise to record inches travelled and elapsed seconds.
Describe how the two measured values affect winning.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher observes actual game and checks both mathematical components.

WorkedExamples.Title: Alternate scoring redesign
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a game use multiplication within100 and addition within1,000?
Steps: A score of3×12=36 is multiplication within100.
Use both operations meaningfully within revised rules.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, if both are used during game
WorkedExamples.Check: Must also test original game at least once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the optional activity as a mandatory new standard.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher explicitly states it introduces no new content standards.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept any two or more distinct valid categories.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source requires test at least once before redesign.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mandate second game test after redesign.
Give one numeric answer for every student's game.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Players set own constraints and rules.

SummaryPoints: Optional source 2021 lesson; warm-up Notice and Wonder carnival game setups.
Groups of four invent rules and win condition; test original game at least once.
Redesign to use at least TWO of: inches, elapsed time, multiplication/division within100, addition/subtraction within1,000.
New-version play and intergroup swap are if-time optional, not core obligations.
Teacher assesses physical game, fair rules, use of math and explanation; no preset winning answer or original source cooldown.
